title: Thermodynamic-limit bootstrap: Solving fractional quantum Hall ground states

paper.title: Thermodynamic-limit bootstrap: Solving fractional quantum Hall ground states
paper.abstract: Abstract Strongly interacting ground states are usually computed in finite systems and then extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit (TDL). Here we develop a quantum many-body bootstrap that solves fractional quantum Hall ground states directly in the TDL. The method gives rigorous and quantitatively tight lower bounds on the ground-state energy and identifies the ground-state structure and topological order. For Laughlin and Pfaffian parent Hamiltonians, it reproduces exact pair-correlation functions and low-lying orbital entanglement spectrum (OES) nearly level by level. For Coulomb interactions, the rigorous TDL energy bounds closely match thermodynamic estimates from exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) extrapolations, and the local diagnostics recover established Laughlin and Moore–Read OES counting and Friedel oscillations of the composite Fermi liquid. Beyond these benchmarks, the bootstrap resolves the thermodynamic ground states at ν = 1 / 4 \nu=1/4 and ν = 12 / 5 \nu=12/5 , identifying a composite Fermi liquid and RR ¯ 3 \overline{\mathrm{RR}}_{3} topological order, respectively. The same framework applies equally well to Abelian and non-Abelian, gapped and gapless quantum Hall states. The TDL bootstrap therefore provides a general ground-state solver that determines both the energy and the state directly in the TDL.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Taken together, these results show that the quantum many-body bootstrap is a ground-state solver directly in the thermodynamic limit. It gives rigorous and quantitatively tight ground-state energy bounds while revealing the local structure of the ground state. Applied to FQH systems, it identifies a composite Fermi liquid at LLL ν = 1 / 4 \nu=1/4 and supports RR ¯ 3 \overline{\mathrm{RR}}_{3} order at LL1 ν = 2 / 5 \nu=2/5 . The price of working directly in the thermodynamic limit is finite correlation range rather than finite system size. ED, DMRG and other finite-system methods are limited by the largest accessible particle or orbital number and approach the TDL by increasing that size. Here the particle number is infinite from the outset; increasing K K instead extends the correlation range R ∼ K ​ ℓ B R\sim\sqrt{K}\ell_{B} . Energy alone would not make the bootstrap a ground-state solver. Although ρ W ⋆ \rho_{W}^{\star} need not be the marginal of any globally realizable state, it reproduces model and DMRG entanglement spectra as well as pair correlations. The bootstrap therefore recovers not only the ground-state energy but also the local structure of the ground state. Competing phases expose a fundamental difference between bootstrap and variational approaches. Variational methods approach the ground-state energy from above and can converge to a competing state that remains higher in energy than the true ground state. The bootstrap instead approaches from below over a larger set of locally consistent density matrices. For the particle–hole-symmetric Coulomb interaction at half filling, Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian orders are exactly degenerate in the TDL, so energy cannot distinguish them and the optimized local state can contain signatures of both. Once this degeneracy is lifted and the bootstrap is sufficiently tight to resolve the energy splitting, the optimized local state should select the structure of the true ground state.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic-limit bootstrap
sections.text: Different from the discussions in the main text, here we detail the constructions of the constraints. Some new notations are needed and properly defined. The bootstrap is formulated directly in the thermodynamic limit (TDL), rather than on a finite system followed by extrapolation. On the Haldane sphere, the n n th Landau level contains 2 ​ l + 1 2l+1 orbitals, with l = Q + n l=Q+n and Q Q the monopole strength. We first take Q , N → ∞ , N 2 ​ l + 1 → ν , Q,N\rightarrow\infty,\qquad\frac{N}{2l+1}\rightarrow\nu, (9) at fixed filling ν \nu . The orbitals near the north pole then approach the symmetric-gauge basis of the infinite plane. We retain a polar window W = { 0 , … , K − 1 } W=\{0,\ldots,K-1\} of K K orbitals, with all matrix elements and constraints evaluated directly in this limit. Thus K K controls the spatial extent of the resolved correlations, not the size of a finite physical system. Increasing K K strengthens the local constraints on the same infinite fluid.

sections.text: The window state is split into ( N W , L W ) (N_{W},L_{W}) blocks of dimensions d b d_{b} , with ∑ b d b = 2 K \sum_{b}d_{b}=2^{K} and largest size d max ≃ 2.2 2 K / K 2 d_{\max}\simeq 2.2\,2^{K}/K^{2} ( 526 526 at K = 16 K=16 ). The number of equality constraints grows approximately as K 7 K^{7} near the largest windows and is dominated by four-body homogeneity: 56,401 56{,}401 of the 62,894 62{,}894 rows at K = 16 K=16 , while the pair and three-body rows grow as K 3 K^{3} and K 5 K^{5} . Each interior-point iteration has two dominant steps. The Newton system for the equality multipliers is a dense n eq × n eq n_{\rm eq}\times n_{\rm eq} Schur complement. The polynomial Schur step dominates up to approximately K ≃ 27 K\simeq 27 ; beyond this point the exponential Fock-space block algebra becomes larger. The iteration count is nearly independent of K K : the K = 10 K=10 – 16 16 calculations converge in 43 43 – 59 59 iterations, and tightening the tolerance adds approximately three to six iterations per decade. A typical K = 16 K=16 calculation requires an order of 100 CPU hours. The present bottleneck is therefore memory in the dense Schur system. Further exploiting sparsity or using iterative SDP solvers can substantially reduce this cost [ 14 ] .

sections.heading: Thermodynamic energy benchmarks.
sections.text: Finite-sphere exact diagonalization uses the Coulomb pseudopotentials of the corresponding Landau level and the relevant shift and parity branches for each filling. We calculate systems with N e = 6 N_{e}=6 – 18 18 electrons, depending on the problem, with the largest calculations containing up to 41 41 active Landau-level orbitals. A uniform neutralizing background with surface charge density σ b = N e ​ e / ( 4 ​ π ​ R 2 ) \sigma_{\rm b}=N_{e}e/(4\pi R^{2}) is included on a sphere of radius R = N ϕ / 2 ​ ℓ B R=\sqrt{N_{\phi}/2}\,\ell_{B} . Let E ee E_{\rm ee} denote the bare electron–electron interaction energy from ED, the density-corrected neutral energy per particle is ℰ N e = ν ​ N ϕ N e ​ ( E ee N e − N e 2 ​ R ) . \mathcal{E}_{N_{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{\nu N_{\phi}}{N_{e}}}\left(\frac{E_{\rm ee}}{N_{e}}-\frac{N_{e}}{2R}\right). (30) The factor ν ​ N ϕ / N e \sqrt{\nu N_{\phi}/N_{e}} corrects the finite-sphere density to the target thermodynamic density [ 39 , 2 ] . The ED energies are extrapolated linearly in 1 / N e 1/N_{e} as shown in Extended Data Fig. 2 . The uncertainty shown in Fig. 2 is the larger of the leave-one-out variation of the extrapolated value and, when available, the difference obtained from an alternative shift or parity branch, and therefore measures sensitivity to the finite-size extrapolation rather than statistical uncertainty. Published DMRG thermodynamic estimates are taken from Refs. [ 65 , 62 ] .

sections.heading: Entanglement-spectrum benchmarks.
sections.text: The Laughlin and Moore–Read reference states are represented as conformal-field-theory matrix-product states constructed from the chiral-boson and boson × \times Ising theories, respectively [ 64 , 10 ] . We use N e = 80 N_{e}=80 electrons, with descendant cutoffs P = 20 P=20 for Laughlin and P = 18 P=18 for Moore–Read and no Schmidt truncation. The same K ′ K^{\prime} -orbital cut is applied to the reference states and to ρ W ⋆ \rho_{W}^{\star} , so the resulting OES can be compared level by level. The independent Coulomb reference at LLL ν = 1 / 3 \nu=1/3 is obtained from finite-sphere DMRG. The calculation uses N = 24 N=24 electrons at N ϕ = 69 N_{\phi}=69 with conserved particle number and L z L_{z} . The OES is the Schmidt spectrum across the cut after the first K ′ K^{\prime} polar orbitals, so it directly matches the orbital cut used for the bootstrap. The displayed spectrum is converged by increasing the MPS bond dimension from χ = 1024 \chi=1024 to 2048 2048 .

sections.text: The Laughlin and Moore–Read model-state pair correlations are evaluated by Metropolis sampling of | Ψ | 2 |\Psi|^{2} on the disk, using N e = 200 N_{e}=200 and N e = 100 N_{e}=100 electrons, respectively. Pair separations are accumulated only from reference particles in the bulk of the droplet to suppress edge effects, and the resulting histogram is normalized by the bulk density to obtain g ⁡ ( r ) g(r) .

Here we develop a quantum many-body bootstrap that solves fractional quantum Hall ground states directly in the TDL. The method gives rigorous and quantitatively tight lower bounds on the ground-state energy and identifies the ground-state structure and topological order. For Laughlin and Pfaffian parent Hamiltonians, it reproduces exact pair-correlation functions and low-lying orbital entanglement spectrum (OES) nearly level by level. For Coulomb interactions, the rigorous TDL energy bounds closely match thermodynamic estimates from exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) extrapolations, and the local diagnostics recover established Laughlin and Moore–Read OES counting and Friedel oscillations of the composite Fermi liquid. Beyond these benchmarks, the bootstrap resolves the thermodynamic ground states at ν = 1 / 4 
u=1/4 and ν = 12 / 5 
u=12/5 , identifying a composite Fermi liquid and RR ¯ 3 \overline{\mathrm{RR}}_{3} topological order, respectively. The same framework applies equally well to Abelian and non-Abelian, gapped and gapless quantum Hall states. The TDL bootstrap therefore provides a general ground-state solver that determines both the energy and the state directly in the TDL. Solving a strongly interacting quantum system requires determining its ground state in the thermodynamic limit (TDL). Most numerical methods approach this limit through finite systems, whose competing states can change relative order with system size. Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems provide a natural setting for this problem. At ν = 12 / 5 
u=12/5 , for example, finite-size corrections obscure the energetic competition between the Abelian Jain state and the particle–hole-conjugate RR ¯ 3 \overline{\mathrm{RR}}_{3} state [ 47 , 66 , 36 ] , as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a). Here we show that the quantum many-body bootstrap solves FQH ground states directly in the TDL. Fractional quantum Hall systems are among the most extensively studied strongly correlated quantum systems, yet many ground states remain unsettled. Exact diagonalization (ED) has been central to identifying FQH phases [ 60 , 20 , 38 , 46 ] ; density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) extends the accessible sizes [ 52 , 13 ] , and iDMRG reaches infinite cylinder length at finite circumference [ 63 , 62 ] . Trial states reach much larger systems [ 28 , 24 , 37 , 45 ] , but require the phase to be chosen in advance. Recently developed neural variational methods are particularly well suited to incorporating Landau-level mixing, but remain limited to system sizes comparable to ED [ 55 , 44 , 1 , 17 ] . In this work, we address this problem with the quantum many-body bootstrap, which replaces a variational wavefunction by universal constraints on local correlations. Positivity, symmetry and consistency conditions on reduced density matrices turn the ground-state problem into a convex optimization [ 34 , 35 , 4 , 22 , 40 , 12 , 8 ] . For quantum Hall systems, one of us previously formulated a bootstrap based on the static structure factor, obtaining rigorous energy bounds and correlation signatures [ 15 ] . That formulation still suffered from finite-size effects and unfavorable scaling, and its particle entanglement spectrum (PES) provided limited state discrimination. More recently, Fock-space positivity combined with rotation averaging yielded rigorous thermodynamic certificates for quantum Hall parent Hamiltonians [ 41 , 16 ] . Here we introduce a direct TDL bootstrap with stronger local constraints that turns rigorous certification into a practical ground-state solver. Here we remove the finite physical system altogether. Discussion Taken together, these results show that the quantum many-body bootstrap is a ground-state solver directly in the thermodynamic limit. It gives rigorous and quantitatively tight ground-state energy bounds while revealing the local structure of the ground state. Applied to FQH systems, it identifies a composite Fermi liquid at LLL ν = 1 / 4 
u=1/4 and supports RR ¯ 3 \overline{\mathrm{RR}}_{3} order at LL1 ν = 2 / 5 
u=2/5 . The price of working directly in the thermodynamic limit is finite correlation range rather than finite system size. ED, DMRG and other finite-system methods are limited by the largest accessible particle or orbital number and approach the TDL by increasing that size. Here the particle number is infinite from the outset; increasing K K instead extends the correlation range R ∼ K ​ ℓ B R\sim\sqrt{K}\ell_{B} . Energy alone would not make the bootstrap a ground-state solver. Although ρ W ⋆ ho_{W}^{\star} need not be the marginal of any globally realizable state, it reproduces model and DMRG entanglement spectra as well as pair correlations. The bootstrap therefore recovers not only the ground-state energy but also the local structure of the ground state. Competing phases expose a fundamental difference between bootstrap and variational approaches. Variational methods approach the ground-state energy from above and can converge to a competing state that remains higher in energy than the true ground state. The bootstrap instead approaches from below over a larger set of locally consistent density matrices. For the particle–hole-symmetric Coulomb interaction at half filling, Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian orders are exactly degenerate in the TDL, so energy cannot distinguish them and the optimized local state can contain signatures of both. Once this degeneracy is lifted and the bootstrap is sufficiently tight to resolve the energy splitting, the optimized local state should select the structure of the true ground state.
